beats.narration: Hola. Softmax turns scores into probabilities — and a common numerical-stability technique is to subtract the maximum first. Today: why that shift doesn't change the answer.

beats.narration: Subtracting the maximum changes the intermediate values, but not the mathematical softmax distribution. It's a numerical safety move. Same math, safer arithmetic. Let me show you why that's guaranteed by the algebra.

beats.narration: Softmax takes a list of scores and turns them into a probability distribution. Higher scores get more mass, lower scores less, and everything sums to one. The rule: exponentiate each score, then divide by the sum of the exponentials. That's the whole recipe.

beats.narration: Here's why. Subtracting c from every score is the same as multiplying every exponential by e-to-the-minus-c. That common factor sits in the top and in the bottom of the fraction — so it cancels. What's left is the original softmax. Algebraically, it's the same expression. The distribution can't change.

shot.visual_intent: SLATE on first previz. FILL step: Manim structured math (MATH-TYPESETTING.md; MathTex, NOT text cards). Four aligned lines, revealed one at a time on cued words, each staying on screen:  (1) p_i = e^{x_i} / Σ_j e^{x_j}   (2) With x_i → x_i − c, c = max_j x_j:  p_i = e^{x_i − c} / Σ_j e^{x_j − c}   (3) = e^{x_i} · e^{-c} / (e^{-c} · Σ_j e^{x_j})   (4) = e^{x_i} / Σ_j e^{x_j}. On the spoken word 'cancels', the two e^{-c} factors in line (3) turn terracotta and cross out simultaneously in numerator and denominator. Ink on cream ground (#FAF9F5). Spark line top: 'The common factor cancels.'

beats.narration: Now the reason we bother. Constructed example — two scores, a thousand and a thousand. The math says the answer is fifty-fifty. Naive softmax needs e-to-the-thousandth. The arithmetic overflows and never gets there.

beats.narration: Shift by the max. Both scores become zero. Exponentiate: one and one. Normalize: point five and point five. The distribution the math promised — computed without ever touching e-to-the-thousand.

beats.narration: So max-subtraction is a numerical trick, not a mathematical change. It avoids unnecessarily large positive exponentials by pinning the biggest score at zero. One honest limit, though. Maximum subtraction avoids unnecessarily large positive exponentials, but this demonstration does not establish that the implementation handles every possible extreme numerical input.
